agent_responses.message: Hi, this is Emma from Atlas Web Studio. I had Acme Dental down as a dental clinic in Phoenix. Am I speaking with the owner or someone who handles the website there?
Yeah, that's me. I handle the website.

Great. I’m calling because we’re putting together a free homepage mockup for a few local businesses, showing how the site could look cleaner and make it easier for patients to take the next step. If we made one for Acme Dental, would you be open to taking a look?
Hmm, a mockup. Can it handle booking, CRM, and payments too?
The free mockup shows the homepage layout and where those features would sit; it does not include working booking, payments, login, or calendar.
So, you're saying Atlas can actually add those features, right? Not just show where they'd go?
Yes, we can build that. It depends whether you need a simple form handoff or a real integration.
Okay, what's the difference between those?

A simple form handoff sends the request details to you by email or into a basic tool, and your team confirms it manually. A real integration connects the site to systems like scheduling, CRM, or payments so information moves automatically. The right path depends on how much you want the website to do without staff handling it.

Yes, we can connect booking and payment tools when the project is scoped for that. The free mockup would still be visual only, so it would show where those entry points sit on the homepage, not the working system behind them.
Okay, so what about the CRM part? Can you guys integrate that too?
Yes, we can build that. It depends whether you need a simple form handoff or a real integration.
Okay, so you can do the real integrations for all three then? Booking, payments, and CRM?

Yes, we can build real integrations for booking, payments, and CRM if the tools support the right connection and the scope is defined. The mockup would just show the homepage direction first, so you can decide whether the layout and patient flow are worth discussing further.

agent_responses.message: Hi, this is Emma from Atlas Web Studio. I had Acme Dental down as a dental clinic in Phoenix. Am I speaking with the owner or someone who handles the website there?
Yeah, that's me. I'm just calling to ask about website prices.

For a typical three to five page new website, our usual range is nine hundred to fifteen hundred dollars. The main driver is whether it is mostly informational or needs things like forms, booking, or integrations. Are you looking for a new site, or changes to an existing one?
Uh, yeah, a new site. But what's the difference between nine hundred and fifteen hundred for a basic one?

The lower end is usually a straightforward brochure-style site with standard pages and content you already have. The higher end is when we need more layout work, copy cleanup, extra sections, or a more polished conversion-focused homepage. For a basic dental site, the free homepage mockup is usually the easiest way to see what direction would make sense before talking about any paid work.
Hmm, so what exactly makes it 'more polished' for the extra six hundred bucks? And what's this free mockup you're talking about?

More polished usually means stronger homepage structure, clearer service sections, better trust signals, cleaner calls to action, and copy that guides patients toward calling or requesting an appointment. The free mockup is a static homepage concept, so you can see the layout and direction before deciding whether a full site is worth discussing. It is not a contract or a payment step.
So what's a 'stronger homepage structure' for a dental office? How does that cost more?

For a dental office, stronger structure means the page is organized around patient decisions: what you treat, why they should trust you, how easy it is to book, insurance or financing cues if relevant, reviews, location, and clear next steps. It costs more when we are not just placing text into a template, but shaping the sections, hierarchy, and wording so the page feels more credible and easier to act on.
Okay, but what specific work are you doing for that extra six hundred dollars?

That extra work is usually custom section planning, homepage wireframing, copy cleanup, visual refinement, and making the calls to action and trust elements fit the practice instead of using a generic layout. It can also include more back-and-forth on the homepage direction before the rest of the site is built. If the site stays very simple and you already have clean content, it may stay closer to the lower end.

agent_responses.message: Hi, this is Emma from Atlas Web Studio. I had Acme Dental down as a dental clinic in Phoenix. Am I speaking with the owner or someone who handles the website there?
Yeah, that's me. I handle the website. I was calling about a CRM integration.Yeah, that's me. I handle the website. I was calling about a CRM integration.
Yes, we can build that. It depends whether you need a simple form handoff or a real integration.
Hmm, what's the difference between those? I already have a compatible site.

A simple form handoff usually means the website collects the request and sends it to you or into a basic tool, while a real integration pushes data directly into the CRM and can trigger workflows or updates. Since your site is already compatible, the right path depends on whether you just need leads captured or actual CRM automation. What CRM are you using?
We use Salesforce. How much would that cost?

For a compatible existing site, a direct CRM integration is usually one thousand to two thousand five hundred dollars plus. The main driver is whether Salesforce just needs new lead records created or whether it also needs field mapping, status updates, and automation. Is it mainly lead capture into Salesforce, or do you need two-way syncing too?
Hmm, I think just lead capture. What exactly is two-way syncing?

Two-way syncing means the website and Salesforce both update each other, so changes in Salesforce can flow back to the site or another connected system. For lead capture, it is usually simpler: the site form sends the new inquiry into Salesforce with the right fields.
Okay, so just lead capture. What would that cost then, specifically?

For lead capture into Salesforce on a compatible existing site, it would likely stay in the one thousand to two thousand five hundred dollars plus integration range. The exact number depends on the number of forms, required fields, validation, and whether Salesforce needs any custom objects or routing rules.
So what would make it closer to the two thousand five hundred dollars then?

It gets closer to two thousand five hundred dollars when there are multiple forms, custom Salesforce fields or objects, conditional routing, validation rules, or testing across several lead sources. If it is one straightforward form creating a standard lead record, it is usually closer to the lighter end of that range.
Okay, so what would make it closer to the thousand dollar mark?

Closer to one thousand dollars would usually mean one existing form, standard Salesforce lead fields, no custom objects, no complex routing, and a clean handoff using an available connector or straightforward API setup. The more the integration needs custom logic or Salesforce-side configuration, the more it moves up.

agent_responses.message: Hi, this is Emma from Atlas Web Studio. I had Acme Dental down as a dental clinic in Phoenix. Am I speaking with the owner or someone who handles the website there?
Yeah, that's me. I'm the owner, and I need a new website for the clinic.

Perfect. The reason I’m calling is we put together free homepage mockups for local clinics so you can see what a cleaner, more patient-friendly site could look like before deciding anything. For Acme Dental, I’d focus the homepage around trust, services, insurance or financing cues, and an easy path for patients to request an appointment. Would you be open to me sending over a free mockup for you to review?
Okay, but I need a whole new site with booking, payments, and a blog. What's the total cost for something like that?

For a new site with standard booking and payment integration, the likely whole-project range is nine hundred to fifteen hundred dollars if it is mostly a three to five page site, but booking and payments can move it into a four thousand to six thousand five hundred dollar range if they need real integration. The main driver is whether those tools are embedded from existing services or custom-connected. Are you using a booking or payment platform already?
What's the difference between "embedded" and "real integration"? We don't use any booking or payment platforms right now.

Embedded usually means we place a third-party booking or payment tool on the site, so patients can use it there, but the tool itself handles the scheduling or transaction. Real integration means the website connects data into another system, like a live calendar, reminders, patient management, or payment workflow. Since you do not have a platform yet, the first step would be choosing whether you want a simple request form, an embedded tool, or a more connected setup.
Hmm, I'm not sure. What would you recommend for a dental clinic like mine?

For a dental clinic, I’d usually start with a simple appointment request path unless you already have a scheduling system you trust. It keeps the site easier to launch, avoids exposing live availability too early, and lets your staff confirm the right appointment type. Payments can often be handled as a separate secure link or embedded tool rather than custom development at the start.
Okay, so if we do that, the simple request form and separate payments, what would the total cost be then?

For a new three to five page site with a simple appointment request form, you are likely in the nine hundred to fifteen hundred dollar whole-site range. A separate payment link or embedded payment button can stay light if it does not need to sync into another system. The main scope driver would be how much content and service-page detail you want included.
Okay, so does that include the blog and the service-area pages I mentioned?

A basic blog setup can usually fit into the site build, but a large set of service-area pages can expand the scope because each page needs content, layout, and local search structure. If it is just a few core pages, it may still stay close to that range; if it is many location pages, we would scope it separately. The free mockup would show the homepage direction first, not every blog or service-area page.
So, if I want a blog and a few service-area pages, is that still in the $900 to $1500 range?

If it is a three to five page site with a blog setup and only a few service-area pages, it may still be close to the nine hundred to fifteen hundred dollar range. The thing that pushes it higher is writing and building many separate local pages. For a dental clinic, I would keep the first version focused and add more local pages once the structure is working.
